items.content:
US consumers are planning to cut back on spending:

The proportion of consumers planning to spend more on restaurants, bars, and take out over the next 6 months fell -2 percentage points in August, to ~24.5%, the 2nd-lowest since September 2025.

US consumers expecting to spend more on health care services fell -3 percentage points in August, to ~19.5%, the lowest since September 2025.

items.title: The world's major central banks have finally unwound most of their pandemic-era balance sheet growth: The Federal Reserve’s total assets as a % of US GDP are down to 21%, the lowest percentage since the 2020 pandemic. items.content:
The world's major central banks have finally unwound most of their pandemic-era balance sheet growth:

The Federal Reserve’s total assets as a % of US GDP are down to 21%, the lowest percentage since the 2020 pandemic.

By comparison, the peak was recorded in 2021 at ~37%.

At the same time, European Central Bank assets as a % of Eurozone GDP fell below 40% for the first time since Q1 2020, from the ~65% peak in 2022.

Total assets on the Bank of Japan’s balance sheet as a % of Japanese GDP are down to ~103%, their lowest since 2020, from the ~130% high in 2021.

The Bank of England’s assets are down to ~21% of UK GDP, the lowest since 2016, from the ~40% peak in 2021.

The pandemic-era central bank stimulus is largely gone.

items.title: Energy stocks have rarely seen this much hedge fund demand: Hedge funds bought the most global energy stocks in almost 4 years last week. This also marks their 12th weekly purchase over the last 13 weeks. As a result, hedge funds are now the most overweight energy relative to global stocks since June 2024. This marks a sharp reversal from their most underweight positioning since 2021, recorded in February 2026. The only period where hedge funds had a materially larger energy exposure relative to global equities was during the 2022 energy bull market. The energy trade is becoming increasingly crowded.

items.content:
The AI boom is transforming Japan's economy.

Japan's exports surged +23% YoY in July, the largest annual increase since October 2022.

This is up from June's +19% gain and marks the 5th consecutive monthly increase in growth.

The surge was driven by electronic component and semiconductor exports, which soared +49% YoY, fueled by demand from AI and data center investment.

At the same time, passenger car exports rose +21% YoY.

Shipments to the US rose +22% YoY, while exports to China and Europe jumped +26% and +19%, respectively.

The improvement also comes as the Yen weakened +11% YoY last month, to a 40-year low against the US Dollar, averaging 161.83, making Japanese exports more competitive globally.

The global AI investment wave is driving a sharp increase in Japanese exports.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) Aug 27, 2026
